summary: Defines a mechanism for building a list of server transport addresses to try when creating a Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) allocation. It uses name lookups to find candidate servers. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: To find a relay helper, you need a list of places to try. This explains how to build that list and in what order to knock.

questions: how to find a turn server
how does a turn client find a turn server
what is the relay service tag in turn
subtitle: How a TURN client turns a configured host name into an ordered list of servers to try, using S-NAPTR and SRV lookups.

tldr.problem: RFC 5766 finds TURN servers with DNS SRV records, but that does not let server administrators provision the preferred transport (UDP, TCP or TLS) between client and server, and does not let the client discover that preference.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an S-NAPTR application with the service tag RELAY and the protocol tags turn.udp, turn.tcp and turn.tls. A five-step algorithm turns four configuration values plus the application's transport list into an ordered list of address, transport and port tuples to try.
tldr.outcome: A TURN client can follow administrator-published DNS preferences, and a provider can point its customers at another company's TURN servers. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 7350 and RFC 8553.

today: RFC 5928 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7350 and RFC 8553, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why TURN Needs a Resolution Mechanism
sections.content:
The TURN specification, RFC 5766, lets a client find TURN servers with DNS SRV resource records. That process does not let TURN server administrators provision the preferred transport protocol between the client and the server, and it does not let the client discover that preference.

RFC 5928 fills the gap with an S-NAPTR application, as described in RFC 3958. The application defines RELAY as the application service tag and turn.udp, turn.tcp and turn.tls as the application protocol tags.

The RFC names a second use, Remote Hosting from RFC 3958. A Voice over IP (VoIP) provider that does not want to deploy TURN servers can use servers run by another company, and still give its customers configuration parameters without showing that relationship. The company hosting the servers keeps managing them as it sees fit.
sections.eli5: Finding a helper is easier if the helper's owner can leave a note saying which door is best. This RFC defines where that note goes and how to read it.

sections.title: Inputs, Outputs and Scope
sections.content:
The mechanism is used only to create an allocation. All later transactions use the IP address, transport and port of the successful allocation. It selects only the transport between the TURN client and the TURN server. The transport of the allocation itself is chosen by the REQUESTED-TRANSPORT attribute from RFC 5766.

There are four inputs, all part of the user's configuration of the TURN client: a boolean <secure>, a <host> that is an IP address or domain name, a <port> that can be empty, and a <transport> that is udp, tcp or empty. A fifth input comes from the application: a list of supported TURN transports (UDP, TCP, TLS), ordered by preference. The output is a list of {IP address, transport, port} tuples to try.

An Allocate error response is processed as a failure, as RFC 3958 describes. Resolution stops at the first successful Allocate response. After success, or after every attempt fails, the resolution context MUST be discarded and the algorithm MUST restart from the beginning for the next allocation. Servers temporarily blacklisted because of a 437, 486 or 508 error code MUST NOT be used for the specified duration, even if a later resolution returns them.
sections.eli5: You give the program a name and a few settings, plus the kinds of doors it knows how to use. It hands back an ordered list of doors to try, and it stops at the first one that opens.

sections.title: The Five-Step Algorithm
sections.content:
First the algorithm checks that the inputs make sense with the application's transport list, and stops with an error for impossible combinations. For example, <secure> true with <transport> udp is always an error, and an unknown transport is an error. If <secure> is true, UDP and TCP are removed from the application's list, and an empty list is an error. Then <secure> and <transport> map to a TURN transport as in the table below.

  1. If <host> is an IP address, use it. With no port, use the default port that RFC 5766 declares for the turn service name (or turns if secure). With no transport, try the filtered transports in preference order.
  2. If <host> is a domain name and <port> is defined, resolve the name with DNS A and AAAA queries. The client picks the order of the resulting addresses in any implementation-specific way.
  3. If <host> is a domain name, <port> is not defined and <transport> is defined, run the SRV algorithm of RFC 2782 with service turn or turns. If the SRV query fails, fall back to A and AAAA queries and the default port.
  4. If both <port> and <transport> are undefined, run S-NAPTR with <host> as the initial target domain and RELAY as the service tag. The ranking of the first set of NAPTR records orders the protocol tags, and the application's own preference breaks ties.
  5. If the first NAPTR query returns nothing, run the SRV algorithm once for each transport in the filtered list.

In every step, if the client cannot contact a server at any returned tuple, resolution MUST stop with an error.
sections.eli5: The program follows five rules, from the simplest case, where you gave it an exact address, to the most flexible, where it asks the name system for the owner's advice. If one rule finds nothing, it moves on to the next.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the first example the application's ordered transport list is {TLS, TCP, UDP} and the parameters are <secure>=false, <host>=example.net, empty port and empty transport. The published DNS records say UDP records come first (NAPTR order 100) and the TCP and TLS records second (order 200). The result is UDP at 192.0.2.1 port 3478, then TLS at the same address on port 5349, then TCP on port 5000.

The second example shows Remote Hosting. A VoIP provider at example.com publishes a single NAPTR record that lists all three protocol tags and points to example.net. The same parameters, with <host> set to example.com, give the same list of tuples as before.

The third example is about compatibility. Where not every client supports this mechanism, the DNS can also carry plain SRV records such as _turn._udp.example.com, _turn._tcp.example.com and _turns._tcp.example.com, so that clients using the RFC 5766 method still work.
sections.eli5: The examples show the owner leaving signs in the name system: first choice here, second choice there. A company can also leave a sign that says 'ask my friend next door', and the program follows it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security for TURN itself is covered in RFC 5766. The new tags add no specific issue beyond those in RFC 3958. That RFC asks an S-NAPTR application to define end-to-end authentication so the client knows it reached the right destination. Here this is done by the Long-Term Credential Mechanism of RFC 5389, which is mandatory for RFC 5766.

Using TLS (RFC 5246) can also meet the requirement. The client MUST then verify the server identity using the procedure in Section 7.2.2 of RFC 5389, with the <host> parameter as the identity to check.

One consequence is that a server's certificate may need to change when SRV or NAPTR records are added. A client configured with turnserver.example.net expects that name in the certificate, while a client configured with example.com expects example.com, even if the SRV record points to turnserver.example.net.
sections.eli5: Before trusting a helper the program checks its name tag, like checking a badge. Because the badge is checked against the name you started with, the helper's owner may need to put several names on it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers one S-NAPTR application service tag, RELAY, and three application protocol tags, turn.udp, turn.tcp and turn.tls, following RFC 3958. Each registration lists RFC 5928 as the relevant publication, points to Section 3 for intended usage and Section 5 for security considerations, and gives the IESG as author and change controller.
sections.eli5: The RFC puts four new names in the official list, so nobody else uses them for something different.

viz.caption: TABLE 1: HOW SECURE AND TRANSPORT MAP TO A TURN TRANSPORT

data.title: DNS records
data.code:
example.net.
IN NAPTR 100 10 "" RELAY:turn.udp "" datagram.example.net.
IN NAPTR 200 10 "" RELAY:turn.tcp:turn.tls "" stream.example.net.

datagram.example.net.
IN NAPTR 100 10 S RELAY:turn.udp "" _turn._udp.example.net.

stream.example.net.
IN NAPTR 100 10 S RELAY:turn.tcp "" _turn._tcp.example.net.
IN NAPTR 200 10 A RELAY:turn.tls "" a.example.net.

_turn._udp.example.net.
IN SRV   0 0 3478 a.example.net.

_turn._tcp.example.net.
IN SRV   0 0 5000 a.example.net.

a.example.net.
IN A     192.0.2.1
